what_this_is: Lean constants whose CONVENTIONS commonly differ from the reading a
natural-language claim invites. `no_unintended_convention` in the
fidelity checklist is a claim about these, and until 2026-10-14 it was a
bare boolean: nothing said which conventions were in play for a given
statement, so a tick carried no information about what was examined.
harness/Audit.lean's `fidelity` mode reports which of these a frozen
statement actually uses, so the tick becomes a claim about a named list
rather than about nothing. Two channels: `conventions_present` for what
the statement itself mentions, `conventions_via_definitions` for what
one of THIS REPOSITORY's own definitions brings in a level down -- the
`Ampas.IsEven` case, where `%` is invisible in the statement.
The names are the ELABORATED ones. Written first against the surface
syntax (`Nat.le`, `Nat.sub`) the list matched almost nothing: `b ≤ a`
elaborates to `@LE.le Nat instLENat b a` and never mentions `Nat.le` at
all. Both forms are listed now, and `statement_constants` in the output
is what the matching was done against, so a miss of this kind is visible
in the record instead of reading as a clean result.

Five rules (`^` associativity, `Nat.pow`, `Nat.Prime`, `Nat.Coprime`) were added after `unmatched_statement_constants` showed `Nat.Prime` and `HPow.hPow` sitting unmatched under three claims -- including the Fermat claim, whose whole content is `2 ^ 2 ^ n + 1` and whose reading depends on `^` associating to the RIGHT. That channel is the only reason the gap was visible; an empty `conventions_present` had read as a clean result.
READ THIS BEFORE READING AN EMPTY LIST. This file is a judgement, not a
derivation: it is the conventions THIS REPOSITORY thought of. A statement
whose trap is not here is reported as using no convention at all, which
is the same failure mode reference/kernel_advisories.json is built
against. `last_reviewed` is what makes an empty result mean anything.

conventions.note: Nat subtraction TRUNCATES at zero: 3 - 5 = 0, so `a - b + b = a` needs b ≤ a.
The same truncation, written directly rather than through the HSub class.
The instance that makes `-` on Nat the truncating subtraction.
Nat division truncates toward zero and n / 0 = 0, so a claim about division needs its divisor constrained.
The same, written directly.
The instance that makes `/` on Nat the truncating division.
n % 0 = n in Lean, which is not every textbook's convention.
The same, written directly.
The instance behind `%` on Nat.
≤ is reflexive, so `b ≤ a` admits b = a; a claim meaning STRICTLY less needs <.
The instance behind `≤` on Nat.
The relation itself, written directly.
On Nat, n < m unfolds to n + 1 ≤ m; a bound stated as < is one tighter than the same number stated as ≤.
The instance behind `<` on Nat.
The relation itself, written directly.
pred 0 = 0, truncating like subtraction.
Every number divides 0, and 0 divides only 0. A claim about divisors usually excludes 0 and may not say so.
The instance behind `∣` on Nat; note `∣` (U+2223) is not the ASCII bar.
A coercion into another numeric type can change which operations' conventions apply.
Lean has three integer divisions (ediv, fdiv, tdiv) that disagree on negative operands.
The matching modulus; its sign convention is one of the three.
Which of the three `/` means on Int.
`^` is RIGHT-associative: `2 ^ 2 ^ n` is `2 ^ (2 ^ n)`, not `(2 ^ 2) ^ n`. A Fermat number is the former; the two agree only at n = 1.
The class instance behind `^`; which `Monoid` it resolves through decides what the base and exponent types are.
The same exponentiation written directly; note 0 ^ 0 = 1 in Lean.
Mathlib's `Nat.Prime` is irreducibility in ℕ: 0 and 1 are NOT prime and 2 is the smallest. A text defining a prime as 'divisible only by 1 and itself' admits 1 and does not match this.
`Nat.Coprime m n` is `gcd m n = 1`, so 1 is coprime to everything and 0 is coprime only to 1.
A numeral's type is inferred, so `2` in a statement may not be the Nat the text means.
The instance that makes a bare numeral a Nat; its absence where a numeral appears means the numeral is something else.

not_covered: Anything not listed above. Known gaps this repository has not written
rules for: real-number conventions (Mathlib's division by zero, sSup of
an unbounded set), List and Array index conventions (get! vs get? vs
getD on an out-of-range index), and the empty-structure cases (a product
over an empty index set, a conjunction over no hypotheses).
A claim using one of those is reported with an empty convention list and
the tick on `no_unintended_convention` then rests on the reviewer alone,
exactly as it did before this file existed.
